A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Reconstructive Visual Instruction Tuning (ROSS). Their readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original ROSS training and evaluation results, including reconstruction-objective ablations, attention statistics, multimodal benchmark comparisons, and SpatialBench transfer experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original ROSS experiments and adds computational measurements, language and high-resolution evaluations, scaling and schedule experiments, and reconstruction analyses.

M1.justification: The core architecture, teacher tokenizer, and reconstruction objectives remain unchanged. Appendix C.2 adds ROSS-7B-anyres, adapting image processing to multiple crops and applying denoising reconstruction to each crop. This changes the input procedure without redesigning the central method.

E1.justification: v2 adds language-only knowledge, commonsense, and instruction-following evaluations through MMLU, HellaSwag, and IFEval, plus a high-resolution input scenario. ImageNet usage expands from tokenizer-fidelity comparison to reconstruction from ROSS features. Document/OCR benchmark names already listed in v1 Table 9 are not treated as wholly new coverage merely because v2 supplies scores.

E2.justification: The existing Table 4 comparator set is retained, while the new high-resolution comparison in Table 13 includes Grok-1.5. The Mini-Gemini-7B row is relabelled Mini-Gemini-8B with identical scores; this alone does not establish a newly evaluated comparison method.

E3.justification: New experimental designs include Qwen2.5 model-size sweeps from 0.5B to 7B using LLaVA-665K, crossed pretraining/instruction-data budgets, high-resolution processing with up to 3,645 visual tokens, and five-epoch ImageNet denoiser fine-tuning. Table 12 also specifies lmms-eval for four VQA benchmarks. These extend the protocols rather than establish changes to the retained default training recipe.

E4.justification: v2 adds denoising-schedule sensitivity tests, language-capability preservation checks, model/data scaling analyses, image-reconstruction probes, and GradCAM visualizations across training. These investigate robustness, interference, scalability, and mechanism. The tokenizer, denoiser-architecture, and attention analyses already present in v1 remain.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains the same attention-distribution percentiles, t-test, Mann–Whitney U test, and p-values. No new repeated-run counts, random-seed reporting, confidence intervals, or benchmark uncertainty estimates are introduced.

E6.justification: Table 4 revises ROSS-7B scores, including MMMU from 43.4 to 46.6, MMVP from 54.7 to 56.7, and POPE from 89.2 to 88.3. Table 3 and several ablation figures also change values. Tables 10–16 and Figures 9 and 12 add substantial numerical and qualitative findings. The PDFs do not explain whether all revised scores reflect corrections or reruns.

T1.justification: The causal-model formulation and objectives in Equations 1–4, and the diffusion definitions and derivation in Appendix A, Equations 5–8, are unchanged. No new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs appear.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal claims about improved comprehension and reduced hallucination remain. The conclusion replaces its closing emphasis on attention and depth understanding with a claim that ROSS features retain sufficient information for image reconstruction, suggesting possible generation without a separate generation expert.

C2.justification: Appendix C.1 adds a substantive hypothesis explaining weaker generative supervision through poor input-target correspondence arising from both datasets and objective design. New discussions address language preservation, scaling, high-resolution applicability, and computational tradeoffs. The original limitation concerning generation capability remains in Appendix D; it was relocated rather than removed.

D1.justification: New disclosures include the eight-A100 setup, training-step count, timing and memory measurements in Table 10, the anyres crop grid and token limit, and the GradCAM layer and target selection. The existing training hyperparameters, dataset-mixture documentation, evaluation prompts, and project URL are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds supporting references for language benchmarks, Qwen2.5, GradCAM, CLIPScore, LAION/MMC4, and alternative noise schedules, plus World to Code in related work. The COCO reference is removed. The central positioning of intrinsic reconstructive supervision against multiple-expert aggregation remains intact.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition is retained. Changes include local paragraph and caption revisions, a rewritten conclusion, renaming Section 5.4 to Applications, organizing Appendix C into four subsections, and moving the discussion to Appendix D. Added contact information and model-name refinements are also limited editorial changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven tables, ImageNet reconstruction examples, and a GradCAM training-evolution figure. Table 4 gains a separate Vicuna-7B block, and some ablation charts change styling. The SpatialBench examples move from main-text Figure 9 to appendix Figure 16, while other existing qualitative figures are regrouped and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses practical-validation gaps in v1 through high-resolution and language-preservation tests, measured training overhead, and sensitivity/scaling controls. However, numerical coherence worsens: v1 consistently reports 59.1 for CLIP/Qwen2 HallusionBench in Figure 7 and Table 3, whereas v2 reports 56.7 in Table 3 and 59.1 in Table 12 without explaining a setting difference. The added validation provides a qualified net benefit, but these reporting inconsistencies limit confidence in the expanded evidence.
